cosy-lesson.title: Why Some Friends Always Try to Correct You

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Compulsion ≠ Self-restraint – an irresistible urge to behave in a certain way.

p.em: Example: She felt a strong compulsion to correct his date.

cosy-blockquote.p: Precision ≠ Inaccuracy – the quality, condition, or fact of being exact and accurate.

p.em: Example: He values mathematical precision in discussions.

cosy-blockquote.p: Pedantic ≠ Casual – excessively concerned with minor details or rules.

p.em: Example: Interrupting every story to fix minor details feels pedantic.

cosy-blockquote.p: Validation ≠ Rejection – recognition or affirmation that a person or feeling is valid.

p.em: Example: Some people correct others to seek intellectual validation.

cosy-blockquote.p: Boundary ≠ Openness – a line that marks the limits of an area or acceptable behavior.

p.em: Example: Setting clear boundaries prevents constant interruptions.

cosy-blockquote.p: Recall ≠ Forgetfulness – the action or faculty of remembering something.

p.em: Example: Human memory recall is naturally selective.

cosy-blockquote.p: Friction ≠ Harmony – conflict or animosity caused by a clash of wills.

p.em: Example: Constant corrections create friction between friends.

cosy-blockquote.p: Rapport ≠ Discord – a close and harmonious relationship.

p.em: Example: Good rapport requires listening without judgment.

cosy-blockquote.p: Nuance ≠ Obviousness – a subtle difference in meaning, expression, or sound.

p.em: Example: Focusing on main ideas matters more than small nuance.

cosy-blockquote.p: Tact ≠ Tactlessness – skill and sensitivity in dealing with others or difficult issues.

p.em: Example: Polite corrections require social tact.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
Why do some people feel a compulsion for absolute precision in informal social stories?
★ Do you ever feel annoyed when someone corrects a minor detail while you tell a story?

Is being pedantic driven by an insecurity or a desire for intellectual validation?
★ Have you ever corrected a friend in front of a group?

How can setting a conversational boundary prevent social friction?
★ How do you react when someone interrupts you mid-sentence?

Why does human memory recall vary so much between two people who witnessed the same event?
★ Have you and a friend ever remembered the exact same event completely differently?

How does maintaining social tact protect daily rapport with close colleagues?
★ What conversational habit do you appreciate most in a close friend?
